The accounts <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Joyce Jeffreys offer a rare opportunity to enter the social world <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the early modern spinster — her daily life, personal circumstances, social activities and family relationships are all reflected through the entries in her manuscript. The accounts also reveal extensive evidence <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Joyce’s business dealings, most prominently as a moneylender in and around the Hereford and Worcestershire region, but also as a farmer, market gardener, landholder, and horse and livestock dealer.

The receipts section includes considerable detail about her loan arrangements and provides evidence <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> rental and other income. The disbursements section offers a wealth <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> information on contemporary expenses, including the cost <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> wages, food, drinks, clothing, textiles, medicines and medical care, the training and care <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> horses, and even stud fees. Further entries relate to amounts paid out in the form <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> gifts and gratuities, litigation fees, local and national assessments, and church dues.

Joyce Jeffreys appears at the centre <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a large, vibrant kinship network. Her business dealings extended beyond county boun- daries as far as London and she travelled regularly to visit relatives and friends, to listen to lectures, and to attend social events. Royalist by inclination, Joyce decided to abandon Hereford before the arrival <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the Parliamentary army and the social as well as economic costs <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the early civil wars are a further feature <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her accounts.

Published in their entirety for the first time, these accounts reveal that Joyce Jeffreys was not as culturally or intellectually isolated as much <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the historiography <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> spinsterhood would have us believe.
Judith M. Spicksley is a Teaching Fellow in the Department <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Economics and Related Studies at the University <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> York.

The series <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Records <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Social and Economic History includes some docu- ments which cover a large geographical area, even the whole country, as in the recent volume <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Diocesan Population Returns for 1563 and 1603. Some <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the documents that we publish, however, relate to a particular place and were produced by an individual. Such documents, which include accounts, journals and letters, are worthy <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> publication in the series because they throw lights on the activities, practices or attitudes <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a whole period or group <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> people. Personal account books are not very common in the mid seventeenth century, so the book kept by Joyce Jeffreys is in itself a rare and valuable survival. It is, however, especially remarkable because it was kept by a woman, and extends beyond the household matters which we are accustomed to find, and reveals much about her business life. As well as making domestic purchases and paying servants’ wages, Joyce Jeffreys managed a farm, but devoted much <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her capital to money lending. We have always known about the importance <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> credit in the economy, before as well as during the period <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> industrialisation, but our information often consists <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> little more than the names <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> lenders and borrowers and the sums owed in inventories or court cases. In this account book we can find out about the loans, the creditors, the interest payments, the length <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the term and the ultimate repayment <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the loan. Historians interested in the credit market everywhere will find useful insights in these accounts, as will those also who work on such themes as religion and the disruptions caused by the Civil War. All <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> this is set in Hereford and the villages around, which is a little studied part <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> England, but is revealed here as a complex society with its own special characteristics.

We are all grateful to Dr Spicksley who has devoted so much time and schol- arship to the preparation <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> this text for publication. Because <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her work Jeffreys can join that select band <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> seventeenth-century individuals—such as Loder, Josselyn and Pepys—whose personal writings tell us so much about the society and economy <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> that period.

Without the financial assistance <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the Economic and Social Research Council <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Great Britain, who granted me a three-year research fellowship in 2001, preparing this edition <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Joyce Jeffreys’ accounts for publication would not have been possible. I am moreover, deeply indebted to the British Library, for granting me permission to publish Joyce’s accounts and to Herefordshire Archive Service, the Bishop <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Hereford, the incumbent <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> All Saints’ Church, Hereford, the unnamed depositor <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the document collection A63/VIII/I-138 and Worcester Record Office, for permission to publish extracts from manuscript documents in their possession.

Preparing Joyce’s accounts for publication has been an illuminating as well as an enjoyable experience, but it would have been much less pleasurable without the interest, support and encouragement <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a great many individu- als. I have been repeatedly uplifted by the generosity <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> people both within and outside the field <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> history who have been willing to share with me their knowledge <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the Hereford area in particular, and <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> early modern England more generally. I must especially thank Craig Muldrew, who read the entire manuscript and suggested a number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> valuable improvements, but the fol- lowing people also made significant contributions at various stages in the project: Charles Hopkinson; Beverly Lemire; Robert Tittler; Mandy Capern; and Mike Turner.

A special vote <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> thanks must also go to the Archivist and staff at Herefordshire Archive Service and at Worcester Record Office, who have fielded my numerous questions with speed and efficiency, and to the staff at Hampton Court Estate, Hope under Dinmore, Herefordshire, who helped me uncover the history <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the house. My husband, Phil, took time off work to chauffeur me around Joyce’s numerous haunts, and the photographs <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Hampton Court and Ham Castle that appear in the volume were taken by him.

For the opportunity to publish Joyce’s accounts, I am especially grateful to the British Academy. Michael (F.M.L.) Thompson responded positively and with charm to an unknown writer, and Joanna Innes not only gave freely <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her time and expertise, but also remained a patient and supportive supervisor to a publishing novice during what turned out to be a rather pro- tracted preparation process; Brigid Hamilton-Jones was immensely patient and helpful in finally bringing the manuscript to publication.

In setting out to edit Joyce’s accounts, I had two distinct aims in mind: to pre- serve as far as possible the look and feel <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the original document; yet at the same time to make the text comprehensible to as wide a range <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> readers as the material might interest. However, finding an appropriate balance between faithfully transcribing the manuscript and making the text easily accessible has called for a considerable number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> editorial decisions that will not delight every reader. In order to retain the look and feel <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the original man- uscript I decided at the outset to adopt a tabularised system <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> editing, and keep the original spelling. Standardisation <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the English language was pro- ceeding hand in hand with an expansion in printing and a rise in literacy dur- ing the early modern period, but the pace was slow until the late seventeenth century.' Thus while there was less variation in seventeenth century letters and diaries than had been the case in their Elizabethan predecessors, consid- erable idiosyncrasy remained. Spelling was much less: uniform in private documents than in printed books and more especially in women’s writing.” In order to assist readers unfamiliar with early modern spelling practices to understand the text, I have included with the glossary a brief discussion <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Joyce’s most common orthographic forms. However, while I have retained the original spelling and layout <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the manuscript, my desire to improve the accessibility <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the text has caused me to move beyond the more usual semi- diplomatic transcription and make the changes described in detail below. I have tried to compensate for this at least in part by incorporating a discussion <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> some <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the characteristics <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the manuscript—within the context <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> developments in the English language—but students <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> early modern lin- guistics, and others with an especial interest in this area, are recommended to consult the manuscript in the British Library.

In editing the manuscript I decided in the first instance to adopt a modern system <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> capitalisation, beginning each new entry with a capital letter, and introducing capitals at the start <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> names, places and feast days. Occasionally the position a man occupied was included as part <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> his name, as in
'G. E. Dawson and L. Kennedy-Skipton, Elizabethan Handwriting 1500-1650: A Guide to the Reading <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Documents and Manuscripts (London, 1966), 16.

‘Mr Maior, James Barroll’, for example, and in these circumstances I have capitalised the first letter <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the position as well as the name. The use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> cap- ital letters often appears arbitrary in the original text, although this can be explained to a large extent by reference to contemporary developments. Between 1593 and 1623 it seems that capitalisation was extended from its link at the former date with certain categories <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> nouns only, to include any form <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> noun, adjective or verb by the latter.’ I have also replaced Joyce’s use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the double lower case ‘ff’ at the beginning <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a word—employed to indicate a capital ‘F’—with the capital itself.

Secondly, though Joyce did add some punctuation to the manuscript, I have re-punctuated the entire transcription, in order to make the entries in the diary as unambiguous as possible. Five types <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> punctuation actually appear in the text: hyphens; colons; parentheses; commas; and periods or full stops. The latter three occur rarely, probably because the manuscript emerges as a set <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> accounts rather than a diary or correspondence, and there are no examples <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> semi-colons, despite the fact that they had been introduced between 1580 and 1590. But Joyce appears to have been particularly fond <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> colons. Prior to the introduction <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the semi-colon, the colon had been utilised to indicate a pause, but it was reinterpreted in the sixteenth century to denote some logical progression or contrary information.* Joyce used colons in her writing for several stylistic purposes: in the curtailment <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> fore- names for example; after numbers and dates; to represent a logical progres- sion; and to separate parts <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the entry. In addition, she occasionally replaced a colon with a dash or hypen, especially where pounds sterling were concerned.

Thirdly I have replaced the inter-changeability <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the characters u and v, and those <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> i and /, with the standard current modern uses <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> these letters (u and i as vowels and v and j as consonants). Originally u and v were differ- ent ways <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> writing the same letter, but in late Middle English it became the norm to use vy when it appeared at the beginning <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a word and wu elsewhere. This was often the format adopted in the printed literature <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, despite the fact that both wu and vy could rep- resent either a vowel or a consonant, and it was not until after 1630 that u and v were used phonetically.° Joyce adopted the Middle English position insofar as she used v for all words beginning with either uv or v, but was less consis- tent about internal examples. The fact that she more commonly used v than u in the middle <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> words when a consonant was required, however, is indica- tive <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the transitional status <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her understanding during the period <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the

manuscript’s construction. This situation is further reflected in her chrono- logical progression towards an increasingly fixed modern employment <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> these characters. However, Joyce did remain consistent in retaining the inter- changeability <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> iand/j. As in the case <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> v and u, the letter j had initially been a different form <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the letter 7. Through the sixteenth century many printers’ fonts included only the single capital form J, but by the second quarter <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the seventeenth century the use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> i as a vowel and j as a consonant had entered writing practice in England.° Joyce’s continued use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> i instead <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> j in the late 1630s and 1640s suggests that the progress <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> this orthographic trend may not been have been as rapid as that <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> its uw and v counterpart, despite its adoption in the printed literature; it must have occurred even later than Gorlach anticipated.’

Fourthly, for ease <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> reading I have expanded all abbreviations in the body <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the text in accordance with accepted conventions, except for a handful <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> well-known examples such as Mr, Mrs and etc.’ I have also retained rece as an abbreviation for received, since it occurs in practically every entry <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the receipt book. Joyce did not employ a bar or any other marks to indicate this contraction, although to be correct she should have done so (see below). And rather than use the standard abbreviation <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> an / crossed horizontally through (for the Latin /ibra) to signify both the pound avoirdupois and the pound sterling as Joyce did, I have inserted /i for pounds sterling, and intro- duced /b for measures <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> weight to avoid confusion. Moreover, I decided to retain abbreviations contained within the marginalia in order to maintain as far as possible the original line format <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the manuscript, but only where the context is either clear from, or repeated in, the main body <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the text. Abbreviations in the form <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> contractions, curtailments (or suspensions), brevigraphs and superscript were a common feature <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> writing during the early modern period, and Joyce’s manuscript is no exception. Most contrac- tions and curtailments were signalled by the appearance <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a bar, known as a tittle or tilde, which in contractions was placed over the whole word in the case <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> large omissions, or above the previous letter where only a single minis- cule, or lower case letter, was missing. The only exceptions to this are Joyce’s occasional apparent arbitrary use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the tilde, in which cases I have rendered the spelling that can be most easily identified, and her nephew’s use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> numbers for autumnal months <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the year, which I have explained alongside in square brackets.

was most often absent, but a bar over a vowel usually pointed to the omission <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> an m or an n, as in fro (from) and upoé (upon), or <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> name endings, <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> which Thé for Thomas was the most frequent. Joyce also used another form <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the tittle, an upward and backward sloping curve from the last written miniscule, in writing abbreviated forms <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the months from September to December (which resulted in the omission <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the final three letters—ber— from the month in question). In addition, she occasionally adopted the hori- zontal crossing through <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the double / to signal a missing e, rather than the tittle.

Like her contemporaries, Joyce adopted the use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> certain brevigraphs or symbols in her writing. In the course <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her text, she employed a vertical elon- gated w rather like the Greek to stand for ir, for example; the y or runic thorn replaced th; a hybrid version <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the secretary/italic ampersand signalled a missing and; and she used a p with a bar through the stem (p) to represent per or par.’ Superscript—used to indicate the omission <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> at least one letter immediately before it—was another abbreviatory technique that became fashionable during the sixteenth century, when it was commonly utilised for forms <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> address, possessive and relative pronouns, and a number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> prepo- sitions. Examples from Joyce’s manuscript include: M’; M”; S’ for Sir; y’ for your; w" for which; w” for with; and finally y’, meaning either that or it, depending on the context. Furthermore, Joyce’s nephew William adopted the symbol’ to replace the letters th in conjunction with dates, even though Joyce herself did not. The symbol itself formed part <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a shorthand technique that developed in popularity during the seventeenth century—it had been used in official records from at least the late sixteenth century—as a number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> authors produced instruction manuals in the art <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> ‘short and swift writing’.!°

Though I have made no changes to the grammatical structure <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the text, a number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> unusual elements call for some brief explanation. For example, in terms <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> her use <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> plurals, Joyce demonstrated considerable confusion over the correct rendition. Sometimes she used the terminal es to indicate a

° The letter y, developed from the runic graph thorn (th), had assumed the role <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the th by the sixteenth century, and survived well into the seventeenth century. Petti, English literary hands, 12. Shorthand was used from the Elizabethan period onwards by lawyers and clerks for case- reports and recording evidence. How and when Joyce learnt to write is not known. 4 The vicars choral existed in Hereford from at least 1237, when there were six vicars in the cathedral church, two in full orders, two deacons and two sub deacons. By 1395 they were twenty-seven in num- ber—a custos and twenty-six vicars—with revenues, laws and a habitation, but they were unable to hold property. Richard II therefore granted them the form and title <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> Collegium vicarorium in choro ecclesie Herefordensis in 1395; they were to have a common seal and as a corporation were able to acquire and hold property. In the following century, however, problems <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> inclement weather and ‘evil doers’ reportedly made it difficult for them to go to church at midnight to celebrate divine service, and in the 1470s they moved from their residence at 29 Castle Street to a new one situated to the east <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the Bishop’s Palace, in the cathedral precincts. During 1534 there were still twenty seven members <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> the college and under Elizabeth in 1583 a royal charter confirmed the vicars in their lands, possessions and rights as a corporation. But in 1637, under royal authority, a revised body <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> statutes was issued that fixed the number <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> vicars at twelve—with the possibility <IA_FTS_MATCH>of</IA_FTS_MATCH> a thirteenth—and four sub-canons.
